title: What coon shouting is and boogie-woogie numbers
summary: He explains that coon shouting is about distinct diction and a solid beat, and lists boogie numbers he sang.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I was going to ask some more about if there's anything else you can tell about the coon shouting style. I mean is it usually pretty loud or is it a part of it?

Well, a coon shouting, no that's where so many people gets confused. They think you have to sing so loud it isn't the loudness. It's the type of voice you have and the style of singing you do and the feeling you put in the song or in the words. And you must pronounce your words very distinctly and put some feeling to them, not just mumble them. As I imagine you noticed in some of my write-ups there that I'm the only singer that doesn't mumble. Yeah, I've heard of that. Or groan or sneeze or sniff or moan or groan or do something. And that's one of the characteristics of coon shouting. You must pronounce your words distinctly. You must have a solid beat and not give up your beat. Just keep stomping and shouting and keep going. And you don't wait for nothing. The musician's got to keep up with you.
Lee, during the 40's what were the name of some of the jazz blues and boogie woogie numbers you sang?
Well, some of the boogie woogie numbers was Cow Cow Boogie and Pig Foot Pete and Beat Me Daddy Eight to the Bar and Scrubbing Me Mama with a Boogie Brush and numbers of that sort.
